# Overview

`ggInterval` extends `ggplot2` for interval-valued data. The package supports
visualizations such as scatter plots, histograms, index plots, radar plots,
line plots, PCA displays, and correlation heatmaps, while keeping the
layered grammar familiar to `ggplot2` users.

This vignette focuses on source-portable examples that can be rebuilt directly
from the package. It uses built-in data, the bundled `data.csv` file for the
aggregation example, and optional sections for packages such as `HistDAWass`
and `MAINT.Data`. The examples below use version 0.2.6; the four diagnostic
functions and `stock.data.LH` are not available in 0.2.5.

An interval-valued observation records an ordered pair of endpoints
$[a_{ij}, b_{ij}]$ for unit $i$ and variable $j$. Its center is
$c_{ij}=(a_{ij}+b_{ij})/2$, its full range is $r_{ij}=b_{ij}-a_{ij}$,
and its half-width is $h_{ij}=r_{ij}/2$. A center alone loses the range.
The endpoints do not, by themselves, specify a distribution of values inside
the interval. Assumptions used by particular summaries are stated below.
The displays support descriptive exploration; they do not establish
recognition accuracy, statistical significance, or estimator superiority.

# Built-in Data

```{r built_in_data}
data(facedata)
data(Environment)

facedata
Environment

Subjects <- substr(rownames(facedata), 1, 3)
Subjects
```

The face data contain 27 cases: nine subjects with three image sequences per
subject and six interval-valued facial measurements in pixels. The stored
values agree, up to printed rounding, with the table reported by Arce Garro
and Rodriguez Rojas (2019). Each interval summarizes one image sequence;
the rule that produced its endpoints is not stated in the inspected sources.
Subject labels therefore identify the recorded cases, without implying a
validated face-recognition procedure.

`Environment` contains 14 symbolic objects, with 13 interval variables and
four modal variables (`URBANICITY`, `INCOMELEVEL`, `EDUCATION`, and
`REGIONDEVELOPME`). The modal fields contain category codes and proportions.
The stored values were compared with the SODAS example distributed with
Umbleja, Ichino and Yaguchi (2020). The original item-to-variable mapping,
endpoint preprocessing, complete codebook, and mapping of the urbanicity
codes remain unresolved. Since 0.2.6 the `INCOMELEVEL` labels follow the
source order 25, 75, 50, 90, 100; earlier versions listed them as
25, 50, 75, 90, 100 with the proportions in the same positions. The
displays below describe stored profiles and do not attach
substantive meanings to the unresolved codes.

# Basic Usage

```{r ggplot2_workflow}
ggInterval_scatterplot(
  facedata,
  aes(x = AD, y = BC, fill = Subjects),
  showLabels = FALSE,
  col = "black"
) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(fill = "Subjects")
```

## Returned Objects and Further Layers

Most plotting functions return ordinary `ggplot` objects. The following
exceptions matter when saving a result or adding layers:

| Function | Returned object | Plot component |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ggInterval_hist()` | `ggInterval_hist_result`, with frequency tables | `$plot` |
| `ggInterval_2Dhist()` | List, with a cell table | `$plot` |
| `ggInterval_PCA()` | Augmented `princomp` object, with `$scores_interval` | `$ggplotPCA` |
| `ggInterval_radarplot(inOneFig = FALSE)` | Arranged grob list | Not an ordinary `ggplot` object |

The histogram result has a print method that draws its plot. Printing a
2D-histogram list displays its nested plot and table; printing a PCA result
shows the PCA summary. `ggInterval_PCA(plot = TRUE)` also draws its plot as
a side effect. To add themes or other layers to these three results, use
the stored plot component, as illustrated later. `scale()` applied to a
symbolic table returns an object whose `$intervalData` component contains
the standardized interval table.

The four diagnostic functions introduced below return ordinary `ggplot`
objects, with computed quantities available through
`attr(plot, "interval_diagnostics")`. They accept symbolic interval tables,
objects containing `intervalData`, or paired numeric endpoint matrices
supplied as `list(lower = ..., upper = ...)`. The `variables` argument
selects interval variables by name.

# Aggregating Classical Data into Interval-Valued Data

The CSV is installed with the package and located with `system.file()`, so
its use does not depend on the working directory. Its empty final column is
read as `X` and removed before excluding the identifier. The K-means output
below illustrates one unseeded run; independently repeated cluster memberships
and summaries can vary, and cluster labels and row order are not fixed.
Diagnosis-based aggregation uses the observed groups and is deterministic.

```{r aggregation_examples}
breastData <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "data.csv",
                                  package = "ggInterval", mustWork = TRUE))
breastData$X <- NULL
breastData <- dplyr::select(breastData, -id)

breastData_kmeans <- classic2sym(breastData, groupby = "kmeans", k = 5)
head(breastData_kmeans$intervalData[, 1:4])

breastData_diag <- classic2sym(breastData, groupby = "diagnosis")
head(breastData_diag$intervalData[, 1:4])
```

# Descriptive Statistics

The center-based mean is supplied by the symbolic methods in `RSDA`.
`sd(facedata)` uses the Billard mixture standard deviation by default; it
includes a uniform-within-interval variance term $h_{ij}^2/3$ and is not the
sample standard deviation of the centers. The explicit `method = "BD"`
below selects the Billard--Diday covariance and its matching correlation
normalization. `B` denotes Billard, and `centers` gives ordinary sample
statistics of the interval centers. Correlations require positive
denominator variances.

`BG` is retained as the software label for Bertrand--Goupil covariance and
correlation. The covariance formula is documented in Irpino and Verde (2015),
Equation (24), where it is attributed to Bertrand and Goupil. The original
Bertrand--Goupil chapter gives univariate means and variances but does not
define a covariance or correlation. The implemented BG covariance is

$$
C_{BG}(X,Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
(c_{Xi}-\bar c_X)(c_{Yi}-\bar c_Y).
$$

The `centers` covariance instead uses divisor $n-1$. The package divides
BG covariance by $\sqrt{C_{BG}(X,X)C_{BG}(Y,Y)}$, giving Pearson correlation
of the centers when their variances are positive. This differs from
Equation (30) of Irpino and Verde, which uses mixture standard deviations
in the denominator. The BG option does not implement the Wasserstein-based
statistics proposed in that article. See `?cov` and `?cor` for formulas and
references.

```{r descriptive_statistics}
mean(facedata)
sd(facedata)

cov(facedata$AD, facedata$BC, method = "BD")
cor(facedata$AD, facedata$BC, method = "BD")

summary(facedata$AD)
summary(Environment[1:3, ])
```

# Univariate Plots

## Index Plots and Index Images

```{r index_plots}
ggInterval_indexplot(facedata, aes(x = AD))

ggInterval_indexplot(facedata, aes(x = AD, fill = Subjects)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(facedata$AD), color = "darkgray") +
  labs(fill = "Subjects")

ggInterval_indexImage(facedata, aes(x = AD)) +
  coord_flip()

ggInterval_indexImage(facedata, aes(x = AD), full_strip = TRUE) +
  coord_flip()
```

```{r index_plot_ordering}
face.ip <- ggInterval_indexplot(facedata, aes(fill = Subjects), plotAll = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(x = "", y = "", fill = "Subjects")
face.ip

b <- ggInterval_indexplot(facedata, aes(fill = Subjects),
  plotAll = TRUE, row_order = "c") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(x = "", y = "", fill = "Subjects")
b

cc <- ggInterval_indexplot(facedata, aes(fill = Subjects),
  plotAll = TRUE, row_order = "r") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(x = "", y = "", fill = "Subjects")
cc
```

In the ordered `plotAll` displays, the outer y-axis labels are suppressed by
default. Here `row_order = "c"` reorders observations by interval centers
within each variable panel, while `row_order = "r"` reorders them by interval
ranges within each variable panel. Set `labels = TRUE` if you want the row
labels repeated inside each variable panel.

## Boxplots and Histograms

The endpoint-quantile boxplots use the empirical 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and
100% quantiles of the lower endpoints and, separately, of the upper endpoints
across observations. The side-by-side view shows the two endpoint
summaries directly. These summaries do not identify the shape of a
within-interval distribution.
The widths of the quantile-box segments are heuristic display weights based
on uniform interval-mass concentration, not an estimated within-interval density.

For the equal-bin histogram, breaks divide the pooled endpoint span into
`bins` equal parts. An interval of positive width contributes its overlap
length with a bin divided by its own width. This allocation corresponds to
uniform mass within each interval: weighted frequencies sum to the number
of observations, and relative frequencies sum to one. A zero-width interval
contributes one to exactly one bin. Bins are left-closed and right-open,
except that the final bin includes the maximum endpoint. A constant variable
uses a support padded on each side by `max(abs(value) * 0.05, 0.5)`.

The one-dimensional `method = "unequal-bin"` display has different semantics.
It counts how many intervals cover each location on a 0.01 grid, joining
consecutive equal counts into rectangles. Its table calls this quantity
`Cumulative.Concepts`; it is a coverage count, not a probability mass or
density. A constant variable is represented by its coverage count at the
exact value as a zero-width rectangle, without grid construction or support
padding. Isolated point intervals can affect a coverage count only at
sampled locations they cover. The `bins` argument is ignored in this mode.

In 0.2.6 the first coverage run is encoded correctly when several intervals
share the minimum. For AD, this changes the first table row from
`[149.35:150.32] 1` in 0.2.5 to `[149.34:150.32] 2`; the positive-width
equal-bin and 2D overlap allocations are unchanged.

```{r boxplots_histograms}
ggInterval_boxplot(facedata, plotAll = TRUE, width_type = "violin-like") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_blank())

ggInterval_boxplot(facedata, plotAll = TRUE, width_type = "side-by-side") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_blank())

ggInterval_boxplot(facedata, aes(x = AD), width_type = "quantile-depth")

hist.obj.equal <- ggInterval_hist(facedata, plotAll = TRUE, bins = 10)
print(hist.obj.equal)
hist.obj.equal$`Table AD`

hist.obj.unequal <- ggInterval_hist(
  facedata,
  plotAll = TRUE,
  method = "unequal-bin"
)
print(hist.obj.unequal)

ggInterval_hist(facedata, aes(x = AD), method = "equal-bin", bins = 10)

ggInterval_hist(facedata, aes(x = AD), method = "unequal-bin")
```

## Line Plot

This example demonstrates the interval-valued line plot using the built-in
`stock.data.LH` table. It contains 62 observations from January--March 1985
in the randomly generated `TTR::ttrc` series, not prices of an actual security.
It can be loaded without TTR installed.

```{r stock_data_preview}
data("stock.data.LH", package = "ggInterval")
head(stock.data.LH)
```

`V1` is the interval `[Low, High]`. The accompanying columns are `Date`,
`Close`, `Low`, `High`, `Month`, and `Day`. `Month` has levels Jan, Feb,
and Mar, and `Day` is the day of month. The interval center is
`(Low + High) / 2`; it need not equal the closing value `Close`.
The vertical ranges and connected centers preserve daily low--high
information, while the added points display the synthetic closing values.
No distribution of prices inside an interval is assumed by this display.
The free vertical scales support reading each monthly panel; they do not
provide a common visual scale for comparing vertical changes between months.
The connecting lines are descriptive, without interpolation of unobserved
daily paths, forecasting, or a financial-performance interpretation.

```{r lineplot_stocklike}
ggInterval_lineplot(stock.data.LH, aes(y = V1, x = Day), barWidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Close), shape = 21, fill = "#D95F02",
             color = "black", size = 1.6, stroke = 0.2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 31), expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Month, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 8, 15, 22, 29)) +
  labs(title = "Interval-valued Line Plot",
       x = "Day of month", y = "Price") +
  ggthemes::theme_economist() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

### Optional Reconstruction from TTR

The following code documents how the stored table was constructed. It is
run only when TTR is installed; the source comparison uses TTR 0.24.4.
The reconstructed object has a separate name so the example does not replace
the built-in data.

```{r stock_data_reconstruction, eval = requireNamespace("TTR", quietly = TRUE)}
data("ttrc", package = "TTR")
stock.data <- subset(
  ttrc[, c("Date", "Close", "Low", "High")],
  format(Date, "%Y-%m") %in% c("1985-01", "1985-02", "1985-03")
)
stock.data$Month <- factor(
  month.abb[as.integer(format(stock.data$Date, "%m"))],
  levels = month.abb[1:3]
)
stock.data$Day <- as.integer(format(stock.data$Date, "%d"))
stock.intervals <- classic2sym(
  stock.data,
  groupby = "customize",
  minData = stock.data$Low,
  maxData = stock.data$High
)$intervalData
stock.data.rebuilt <- dplyr::bind_cols(stock.intervals, stock.data)
head(stock.data.rebuilt)
```

# Bivariate Plots

## Scatter Plot with Label Controls

```{r scatterplot_labels}
ggInterval_scatterplot(
  facedata,
  aes(x = BC, y = AD, fill = Subjects),
  showLabels = TRUE,
  labelSize = 2.6,
  labelPosition = "topright",
  labelNudgeX = -0.2,
  labelNudgeY = 0.15,
  checkOverlap = FALSE,
  color = "black"
) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.06, 0.10))) +
  labs(fill = "Subjects")
```

## 2D Histograms

Both 2D methods allocate each observation's mass as the product of the two
axis-overlap fractions. For positive-width intervals, this is the product
of uniform distributions within the observation's rectangle. `display = "f"`
shows weighted frequencies, `"p"` shows relative frequencies, and `"h"`
shows relative frequency divided by cell area. The relative frequencies sum
to one; for density, the sum of density times cell area is one. A point on
an axis is assigned to exactly one bin using the same boundary convention
as the equal-bin one-dimensional histogram.

Here `method = "unequal-bin"` uses sorted unique endpoints, with `tau`
merging chains of adjacent gaps smaller than that tolerance while retaining
the outer endpoints. It still displays allocated mass or density, unlike
the one-dimensional unequal-bin coverage-count display. A constant axis is
padded by the same rule as above. Displayed table endpoints and values are
rounded, whereas allocation uses unrounded values.

```{r hist2d_equal}
face.2dh.equal <- ggInterval_2Dhist(
  facedata,
  aes(x = BC, y = AD, col = "white"),
  method = "equal-bin",
  xBins = 10,
  yBins = 10,
  display = "p",
  palette = "Blues",
  direction = 1,
  cell_labels = TRUE
)$plot

face.2dh.equal +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1)
```

```{r hist2d_unequal}
face.2dh.unequal <- ggInterval_2Dhist(
  facedata,
  aes(x = BC, y = AD, col = "white"),
  method = "unequal-bin",
  display = "p",
  palette = "Blues",
  direction = 1,
  tau = 0.5
)$plot

face.2dh.unequal +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1)
```

## Radar Plots

For the mixed `Environment` profiles, each interval axis is normalized by
that variable's observed endpoint range over all 14 objects. Radial widths
are therefore relative ranges, not directly comparable raw widths across
variables. Modal bars occupy the stored category positions; their heights
increase with the proportions but are not proportional to them. The default
polygon passes through the largest-proportion category. The missing
codebook described above prevents label-specific interpretation.

The `type = "quantile"` examples pool lower and upper endpoints for each
interval variable. With `quantileNum = q`, they retain empirical quantiles
at $k/(q+3)$ for $k=1,\ldots,q+2$, round to two decimals, and pair adjacent
quantiles into $q+1$ bands. Each axis is normalized over its retained quantile
range. These are adjacent pooled-endpoint bands, not nested central-coverage
intervals, confidence bands, or distributions inside the individual intervals.
They do not directly compare absolute spread or establish skewness.

```{r radar_plots}
library(ggthemes)

ggInterval_radarplot(
  Environment,
  plotPartial = c(4, 6),
  showLegend = FALSE,
  base_circle = FALSE,
  base_lty = 1,
  addText = FALSE,
  addText_modal = FALSE
) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkred", "darkblue")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkred", "darkblue")) +
  labs(title = "") +
  theme_hc()

ggInterval_radarplot(
  Environment,
  plotPartial = c(4, 6),
  showLegend = FALSE,
  base_circle = FALSE,
  base_lty = 1,
  addText = FALSE,
  addText_modal = FALSE,
  type = "rect"
) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkred", "darkblue")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkred", "darkblue")) +
  labs(title = "") +
  theme_hc()

ggInterval_radarplot(
  facedata,
  base_circle = FALSE,
  base_lty = 1,
  type = "quantile",
  quantileNum = 5,
  showLegend = TRUE,
  Drift = 0
) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greys") +
  labs(title = "", fill = "Quantiles") +
  theme_hc()

ggInterval_radarplot(
  Environment,
  base_circle = FALSE,
  base_lty = 1,
  type = "quantile",
  quantileNum = 5,
  showLegend = TRUE,
  Drift = 0
) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greys") +
  labs(title = "", fill = "Quantiles") +
  theme_hc()
```

# Customization

```{r customization_examples}
set.seed(1234567890)
facedata.tmp <- facedata
facedata.tmp$cluster <- RSDA::sym.kmeans(facedata.tmp, k = 3)$cluster

ggInterval_indexplot(facedata.tmp, aes(y = AD, fill = Subjects)) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = seq_len(nrow(facedata.tmp)), y = .data$AD$min,
        label = rownames(facedata.tmp)),
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Customized Index Plot Using K-Means Clusters",
       fill = "Subjects") +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(cluster), scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  theme_economist_white() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

# Working with Other SDA Packages

## Histogram-Valued Data via HistDAWass

This example is evaluated only when the optional package `HistDAWass` is
installed.

```{r histdawass_example, eval = requireNamespace("HistDAWass", quietly = TRUE)}
BLOOD <- HistDAWass::BLOOD
blood.min <- HistDAWass::get.MatH.stats(BLOOD, stat = "min")
blood.max <- HistDAWass::get.MatH.stats(BLOOD, stat = "max")
blood <- data.frame(blood.min, blood.max)

myBLOOD <- classic2sym(
  blood,
  groupby = "customize",
  minData = blood[, 2:4],
  maxData = blood[, 6:8]
)

colnames(myBLOOD$intervalData) <- HistDAWass::get.MatH.main.info(BLOOD)$varnames
ggInterval_PCA(myBLOOD$intervalData, plot = FALSE)$ggplotPCA
```

## Midpoint-Range Data via MAINT.Data

This example is evaluated only when the optional package `MAINT.Data` is
installed.

```{r maint_data_example, eval = requireNamespace("MAINT.Data", quietly = TRUE)}
AbaloneIdt <- MAINT.Data::AbaloneIdt

AbaloneRange <- exp(AbaloneIdt@LogR)
AbaloneMid <- AbaloneIdt@MidP
AbaloneBounds <- data.frame(
  AbaloneMid - AbaloneRange / 2,
  AbaloneMid + AbaloneRange / 2
)

myAbalone <- classic2sym(
  AbaloneBounds,
  groupby = "customize",
  minData = AbaloneBounds[, 1:7],
  maxData = AbaloneBounds[, 8:14]
)

colnames(myAbalone$intervalData) <- AbaloneIdt@VarNames
ggInterval_PCA(myAbalone$intervalData, plot = FALSE)$ggplotPCA
```

# PCA and Correlation Heatmaps

These examples use vertex-based interval PCA. In `ggInterval_PCA()`, vertex
coordinates are standardized column-wise before `princomp`; retained
vertices receive equal weight. This treats the vertices as the input to the
projection, without specifying a distribution inside each box. Projected
intervals and polygons describe geometric spread and overlap, not confidence
regions, recognition accuracy, or significance. The returned object is an
augmented `princomp` result; add graphical layers to `$ggplotPCA`.

```{r pca_example}
pca.results <- RSDA::sym.pca(facedata, method = "tops")
pca.results$Sym.Components <- structure(
  as.data.frame(pca.results$Sym.Components),
  class = c("symbolic_tbl", "data.frame"))
rownames(pca.results$Sym.Components) <- rownames(facedata)

ggInterval_scatterplot(
  pca.results$Sym.Components,
  aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, fill = as.factor(Subjects)),
  labelSize = 2.6,
  labelPosition = "topright",
  labelNudgeX = -0.2,
  labelNudgeY = 0.15,
  checkOverlap = TRUE,
  col = "black"
) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.06, 0.10))) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  labs(x = "PCA-1", y = "PCA-2", fill = "Subjects")

face.pca <- ggInterval_PCA(
  facedata, poly = TRUE, concepts_group = as.factor(Subjects), plot = FALSE
)
face.pca$ggplotPCA +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  labs(x = "PCA-1", y = "PCA-2")
```

The heatmap below uses the package's BG normalization described above.
It is a heatmap of interval-center Pearson correlations, not the
center--range association map introduced in the next section.

```{r corrplot_example}
ggInterval_corrplot(facedata, method = "BG", triangle = "lower")
```

# Graphical exploration of simulated interval-valued data

The following data reproduce the generating mechanism and seed used in the
paper's simulation. They contain three groups of 15 bivariate observations.
Within each group, the two center coordinates have unit generating variances
and generating correlation 0.7, with means `(0, 0)`, `(6, 5)`, and `(-5, 6)`.
Independent half-widths are initially uniform on `[0.2, 0.9]`, `[0.2, 1.4]`,
and `[0.2, 1.9]` for the three groups. Three selected observations have both
half-widths increased by 4; their centers are unchanged. The generated data,
not a newly tuned scenario, are shared by all four diagnostic examples.

```{r simulation_data}
set.seed(20260709)

sim_interval <- function(n_per = 15, rho = 0.7,
                         mu = list(c(0, 0), c(6, 5), c(-5, 6)),
                         hw_lo = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2),
                         hw_hi = c(0.9, 1.4, 1.9),
                         outlier_frac = 0.06) {
  G <- length(mu)
  Sigma <- matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2, 2)
  rows <- list()
  for (g in seq_len(G)) {
    C <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_per, mu = mu[[g]], Sigma = Sigma)
    h1 <- runif(n_per, hw_lo[g], hw_hi[g])
    h2 <- runif(n_per, hw_lo[g], hw_hi[g])
    df <- data.frame(
      group = factor(g),
      X1min = C[, 1] - h1, X1max = C[, 1] + h1,
      X2min = C[, 2] - h2, X2max = C[, 2] + h2)
    rows[[g]] <- df
  }
  dat <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  # Move both endpoints outward by 4; preserve the centers.
  n_out <- max(1, round(outlier_frac * nrow(dat)))
  idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(dat)), n_out)
  dat$X1min[idx] <- dat$X1min[idx] - 4; dat$X1max[idx] <- dat$X1max[idx] + 4
  dat$X2min[idx] <- dat$X2min[idx] - 4; dat$X2max[idx] <- dat$X2max[idx] + 4
  dat$outlier <- FALSE; dat$outlier[idx] <- TRUE
  dat
}

sim <- sim_interval()
sim.sym <- classic2sym(sim, groupby = "customize",
                       minData = sim[, c("X1min", "X2min")],
                       maxData = sim[, c("X1max", "X2max")])$intervalData
colnames(sim.sym) <- c("X1", "X2")

which(sim$outlier)
centers <- data.frame(group = sim$group,
                     X1 = (sim$X1min + sim$X1max) / 2,
                     X2 = (sim$X2min + sim$X2max) / 2)
round(c(pooled = stats::cor(centers$X1, centers$X2),
        sapply(split(centers, centers$group),
               function(d) stats::cor(d$X1, d$X2))), 3)
```

The injected rows are 6, 10, and 39. The within-group sample correlations
are approximately 0.86, 0.89, and 0.65; the pooled sample correlation is
approximately -0.08. The latter also reflects differences among group means.
Neither the generating correlation nor these sample correlations is an
intraclass correlation or a measure of agreement between study centers.
Here an interval center simply means its midpoint.

## Endpoint ECDF Envelope

```{r diagnostic_ecdf}
p.ecdf <- ggInterval_ecdf(sim.sym, variables = "X1")
p.ecdf
head(attr(p.ecdf, "interval_diagnostics")$knots)
```

The lower curve is the empirical CDF of the upper endpoints and the upper
curve is the empirical CDF of the lower endpoints. Every empirical CDF
formed by selecting one value per interval lies between them, with equal
observation weights. Steps and shaded rectangles use exact endpoint knots;
the dashed line is the midpoint ECDF. This is an endpoint envelope, not a
confidence band or an estimated within-interval distribution.

## Center--Range Association Map

```{r diagnostic_association}
p.association <- ggInterval_CRcor(sim.sym, group = sim$group)
p.association
association <- attr(p.association, "interval_diagnostics")
round(association$pooled, 3)
round(association$group_demeaned, 3)
```

For each variable this display derives a center column `C` and a full-range
column `R`. The lower-left triangle contains ordinary Pearson correlations
pooled over observations. With `group` supplied, the upper-right triangle
uses residuals after removing each group's mean from each derived column.
The diagonal contains pooled self-correlations. This juxtaposition helps
separate pooled associations from associations after group-mean removal;
the assembled display is not a single correlation matrix.

Group-demeaned correlations are not averages of group-specific correlations,
ICCs, inter-center agreement measures, or the B, BD, or BG interval
correlations. A constant derived column has undefined correlation, shown as
`NA`. Group labels are supplied information, not estimated clusters.

## Center--Range Deviation Contributions

```{r diagnostic_deviation}
p.deviation <- ggInterval_deviation(
  sim.sym, group = sim$group, highlight = sim$outlier
)
p.deviation
head(attr(p.deviation, "interval_diagnostics")$contributions)
```

The default reference comprises componentwise medians of the centers and
full ranges within each supplied group; the default scale for each variable
is its global endpoint span. With center difference $\Delta c_j$, full-range
difference $\Delta r_j$, and positive scale $s_j$, the two contributions are
$\sum_j(\Delta c_j/s_j)^2$ and
$\sum_j(\Delta r_j/(2s_j))^2$. Their sum equals the mean squared standardized
deviation of the two endpoints, summed over variables.

Bars are ordered by total deviation and retain every observation. Outlined
bars identify the supplied injection labels; the function does not detect
outliers. This is a geometric decomposition, not a Shapley attribution or
a calibrated test. Values depend on the chosen reference and scales, so a
large bar should be interpreted with its center and range contributions.

## Pairwise Box Overlap

```{r diagnostic_overlap}
p.overlap <- ggInterval_overlap(sim.sym, group = sim$group)
p.overlap
attr(p.overlap, "interval_diagnostics")$overlap[1:5, 1:5]
```

Each observation is the Cartesian product of its selected intervals. A cell
shows intersection volume divided by union volume: zero for disjoint boxes
or mere boundary contact and one for identical positive-volume boxes.
Grouping changes the display order, not the overlaps. This compares
observations geometrically; it is not a variable-correlation heatmap or a
measure of agreement between unobserved within-box distributions.

Any box with zero width on a selected axis has zero volume. The default
`zero_width = "error"` rejects this case; `zero_width = "na"` marks every
pair involving that box as missing, including its diagonal. It does not
assign artificial zero or perfect overlap to degenerate boxes.
